chapter: Army service and after the war
title: The union rules he must pay for missed dates
summary: After the war the union made McShann pay four promoters for missed dates because Tomino had not informed them.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well, now, though, the contracts that you had on those one-nighters, when Uncle Sam moves in, that just voids everything, doesn't it?
Well, I'll tell you what happened. I told Johnny, I says, Johnny, if the guys are not going to make these dates, I says, contact everybody and let them know that I went in the service.

Okay. Well, he was trying to get these dates, and I still -- they took me to the National on about three or four dates, and did you know that they made me pay? Yes, they did. A date in Cincinnati, a date in Youngstown, about four dates.
When did they make you pay?
After I came out of the service and organized again. That's the union. And the union -- I told them that, damn it, I was in the service. And gave them the
proof. And they ruled against me, and they made me pay these four guys that said they lost so much money on the deal.
Well, that seems kind of ridiculous, because you didn't know when you'd be hauled into the Army, did you?
No. They said that I didn't contact them and let them know.
He didn't take care of it, did he, John?

No, he didn't. And then on the other hand, too, I don't see how -- even though he didn't contact them, how they could rule that against me. You know what I mean? They know the date, and I gave me the date that they picked me up and took me in the service. So they knew. And in other words, consequently that's just -- that stands for itself, even though Johnny didn't contact these people or the rest of the people until -- but I never did understand that. But the union ruled in favor.
